Yes, Tesla is deploying Robotaxi very slowly for some reason. However, Tesla is constantly producing new Cybercabs, and those are filling parking lots at a stable rate. Recently, new Cybercabs reportedly no longer have steering wheels, according to @tesla2moon.

If the large-scale deployment timeline is unclear to Elon, then why doesn’t he pause or slow down Cybercab production, or at least add steering wheels to them?

In fact, if you think about Robotaxi long term, the scaling rate will probably be bottlenecked by the manufacturing rate for years. So I suggest that, in the early stages, we look at the production rate of Cybercabs, especially those without steering wheels, to estimate the actual “scale” of Robotaxi, instead of only looking at those running on the road. This might reduce short-term noise.

This is another similar scenario. The first part is almost identical, but the second half is far more dangerous than mine.

When an event is unfolding in real time, there are multiple plausible futures with similar probabilities. FSD cannot assume the best-case outcome. In this video, the other driver actually accelerated into the lane and created an extremely dangerous situation.

What’s interesting is that FSD made almost the same magnitude of evasive maneuver in his video as it did in mine. That suggests FSD was not overreacting in my case. It was choosing a “Game theory Optimal”-style strategy: instead of betting on what the reckless human driver would do next, it positioned itself to preserve safety across multiple possible outcomes.

This is the kind of strategy humans often fail to appreciate, because humans judge the event after seeing how it ended.

I gave it more thought, and I think I found all the answers. I have to say SpaceX’s story is much harder to comprehend compared with Tesla’s.

The short answer is that 1) inference is trending toward becoming the majority of future compute expense. One day, training in space might also make economic sense. 2) Sending AI chips to space does not make compute cheaper in absolute terms, but during a severe shortage, it can make adding new compute less expensive relative to ground-based alternatives. And 3) to make the AI story complete, Terafab must succeed in solving the production capacity issue around memory and packaging. Hopefully, faster iteration is the key to addressing that challenge, but the risk remains.


Raines (@raines1220)

Please correct me if I’m wrong, but here are my thoughts about AI satellite from SPCX:

1. Training/inference: They are kilometers away from each other. Due to physics limitations, the latency and bandwidth between satellites will make them better suited for inference only, not training.

2. Energy saving: Energy cost for data centers is usually less than 10%. The majority of data center cost today is still depreciation of AI chips. Therefore, even if you consider energy cost as zero, I still have trouble seeing significant cost efficiency when comparing on-ground data centers with in-space ones.

3. Production capacity: If AI chip manufacturing speed is the scaling bottleneck, then launching AI satellites does not unblock scaling, since the satellites still need to wait for the chips. Otherwise, the plan to have 10,000 Starship launches per year becomes the bottleneck, and at this speed, it still does not significantly outpace the expected compute scaling speed on the ground within five years.
